title: The surveillance workplace is here
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Karian argues that workplace monitoring has already won on adoption and has never been argued for on the merits, and he sets out to close that gap. He opens with a bank that emailed staff warnings about unaccounted activity including bathroom breaks, withdrew the software within days, and left the underlying instinct fully intact. He then assembles the counter-evidence: stress running far higher in heavily monitored settings, three in four workers reporting lower job satisfaction, and monitored employees nearly twice as likely to plan an exit within the year. His sharpest point is a substitution effect. Surveillance produces better-looking work rather than better work, and because the cost of that substitution cannot be measured, organisations keep measuring everything else instead. He adds a legal warning that most employers have not read the 2023 ICO guidance closely enough to know how exposed they are, citing the CNIL fine against Amazon France as a structural rather than exceptional case. The cultural argument is the one he treats as decisive: monitoring sends a message of distrust that cannot be unsent, and the discretionary effort high-trust teams produce does not travel through surveillance systems. He concedes that transparent, proportionate monitoring with genuine employee involvement is defensible, and denies that this is what most organisations are actually doing.
points: Seventy-four percent of surveyed employers now run online tracking, three-quarters monitor physical space, and 61 percent use AI analytics to score behaviour.
Monitoring reliably buys visible activity rather than output, and 72 percent of employees say it does nothing for their productivity or actively reduces it.
Retention is the unpriced cost: 42 percent of monitored employees expect to leave within a year against 23 percent of unmonitored peers.
The ICO requires a lawful basis and a Data Protection Impact Assessment for keystroke logging and automated performance decisions, and warns explicitly against function creep.
Karian concedes a defensible version of monitoring that is transparent, proportionate and built with employees, and argues almost nobody is running it.
quotes: In 2020, a large multinational installed software that emailed staff daily updates warning them when they had been ‘not active enough’ or had ‘too many unaccounted activities’, including bathroom breaks.
According to a February 2025 survey of 1,500 employers, 74% now use online tracking tools including real-time screen monitoring and web browsing logs.
Employees in high-surveillance environments (combining online and physical monitoring) report stress levels of 45%, compared with 28% in less monitored settings.

What monitoring reliably produces is not better work but better-looking work (more keystrokes, more visible activity, more movement on the productivity dashboard) while employees channel energy into appearing productive rather than being productive.
The ICO’s position is clear: monitoring must be proportionate, transparent, and necessary.
The signal is: we do not trust you to do your job without watching you. That signal, once sent, is extraordinarily difficult to unsend.
They are probably right that enforcement is patchy. That is not the same as compliant.

An employee who knows their keystrokes are being logged, their idle time is being flagged, and their productivity score is being algorithmically generated does not experience a high-trust environment.
